title: Verbal tips and tricks
lines: Verbal Reasoning rewards careful reading more than a huge vocabulary. The words matter, but the questions are designed so that the sentence or passage itself tells you what is needed. These habits help across all the Verbal types.
## Text Completion
- Cover the choices and read the whole passage first. Choices read too early pull you toward traps.
- Find the clue: a phrase that describes or explains the blank.
- Find the signal word. Same direction: "and", "because", "in fact", "indeed", a colon or semicolon. Opposite direction: "although", "but", "yet", "despite", "however", "rather than".
- Predict a simple word of your own, then match it to the choices.
- In multi-blank items, start with the blank that has the strongest clue, which is often not the first one.
- Reread the full passage with your choices in place. Every blank must fit together.
> Despite the reviewer's _____ tone, her conclusions were surprisingly generous.
> Signal: "Despite" shows contrast with "generous". Prediction: harsh. A word like "caustic" fits.
! A choice that sounds sophisticated is not more likely to be right. The answer is the word that fits the logic.
## Sentence Equivalence
- Predict the meaning of the blank before you look.
- Find all choices that match your prediction. You need exactly two that fit and make sentences with the same meaning.
- Watch for a pair of synonyms that does not fit the sentence. It is a common trap.
- Watch for a single word that fits well but has no partner among the choices. If no other choice means the same, it is not part of the answer.
- If you find only one good word, look for a second word that is close in meaning even if it is less familiar.
## Reading Comprehension
- Read for structure: What is the main point? What does each paragraph do (introduce, support, contrast, conclude)?
- Note the author's attitude. Words such as "unfortunately", "surprisingly" or "rightly" reveal it.
- Answer from the passage, not from what you know about the topic. A choice can be true in the real world and still wrong.
- Prefer moderate choices. Answers with "always", "never", "only" or "completely" are often too extreme for what the passage supports.
- For "select one or more" questions, judge each choice on its own. Any number from one to three can be correct.
- For select-in-passage questions, read the question carefully and test the sentences in the named part of the passage one by one.
> Typical wrong answers: too extreme, out of scope, the reverse of what is stated, true but not relevant to the question, or half right and half wrong.
! If two choices both seem right, find the single word in one of them that the passage does not support. That word makes it wrong.
## Argument paragraphs
- Find the conclusion first, then the evidence for it.
- Look for the gap between evidence and conclusion. Assumption, strengthen and weaken questions are all about that gap.
- To weaken, look for another explanation of the evidence. To strengthen, rule one out.
- For boldface questions, label each bold part: conclusion, evidence, an opposing view, or a fact the author explains.
## Building vocabulary that pays
- Learn words in context, with a sentence, not as isolated lists. The flashcards in this app each come with an example sentence and synonyms.
- Group words by meaning: words for praise, for criticism, for "changing a lot", for "stubborn". Synonym groups are exactly what Sentence Equivalence tests.
- Study a little every day. Fifteen minutes of flashcards daily beats two hours once a week.
- Learn second meanings of common words. On the GRE, "qualify" can mean "limit", "check" can mean "restrain" and "temper" can mean "moderate".
- Learn common roots: "bene-" good, "mal-" bad, "-loqu-" speak, "chron-" time. They help you guess unfamiliar words.
## When you do not know a word
- Decide whether it feels positive or negative from its roots or from words it resembles.
- Eliminate choices you know are wrong, then guess among the rest.
- Never leave a question blank, and do not spend long on a question that depends on one unknown word.
## Practice plan in the app
- Each Verbal topic has a lesson and a practice set. Do the lesson once, then do the set, then read every explanation, including for questions you got right.
- Keep a list of words you missed and add them to your flashcard review.
- In mocks, check whether your Verbal errors come from vocabulary, from reading or from timing. Each needs a different fix.
